Water Generator: water bodies built with nodes

Stable Doppio Last updated: 2026-11-20

Assemble lakes, rivers, seas and storms from a node graph and place them as an animated engine water surface.

The Water tab (View menu, next to Nature) builds lakes, rivers, seas and storms from a node graph and places them in the scene as an animated engine water surface. It replaces the old fixed wind-wave block: waves are now data you assemble, and the same waves drive the editor preview, the engine mesh and gameplay queries (water_height, for floating objects).

1. How a graph works#

Two typed ports (two colours); a link only connects ports of the same type and never closes a cycle:

Port Carries
Waves a list of Gerstner waves (direction, wavelength, amplitude, steepness, phase)
Look the Water Material: colour, opacity (low = clear), roughness and foam threshold
Category Nodes
Waves Gerstner Wave (one explicit wave), Wind Sea (a spectrum from wind speed, direction, spread and choppiness), Swell (long regular trains from afar), Ripples (short waves from many directions)
Modifiers Merge Waves (up to four sources; keeps the strongest 16), Scale Waves (amplitude, wavelength, choppiness, rotation)
Look Water Material
Output Output: size X/Z, water level, depth, mesh resolution, time scale, seed

Interaction is the same as the other generators: palette on the left, canvas in the middle, parameters and the animated Surface preview on the right. Undo/redo cover every edit, Export writes Water/<name>.generator.water (a recipe wrapping the CAFWATER1 / WATERGRAPH1 text), Place in scene creates the entity. The preview is a top-down render of the same Gerstner sum the engine animates (sun-lit slopes, a Fresnel sky reflection, foam where crests compress); it is a shape preview, not the final shading.

1b. The water always has its material#

Water cannot exist without a material: the Output's Material port needs a Water Material node, and a graph without one does not build ("The water has no material: wire a Water Material node..."). Place in scene writes that node as a real project asset, Water/<name>.mat (colour and opacity, roughness, a low base reflectance, a thin clearcoat, transmission and the refraction index of water, alpha blend), and assigns it to the water entity, so the material is visible in the Assets panel and editable in the Material tab like any other. The engine renders the water with the entity's material whenever it has one (without a material it falls back to a built-in water look). Placing again regenerates the .mat from the node; keep your edits by assigning your own material afterwards.

2. Why this is modular and cheap#

  • Waves are the unit of work. A sea is a handful of well-chosen waves, not a texture or a simulation. The engine evaluates at most 16 explicit waves on a vertex-displaced mesh, so the cost is vertices x waves regardless of how you built them. Merge keeps the strongest; the Gerstner stability bound (sum(Q k A) < 1, crests never fold over themselves) is enforced by the sources and tested.
  • One model for everything. Lake, river, pool and ocean differ only in graph and Output: a river is two stretched waves along the flow plus cross ripples; a storm is a gale-driven spectrum plus a tall swell.
  • Gameplay can sample it. caffeine_session_water_height(entity, x, z) returns the simulated surface height, so boats and floating objects follow the same waves you see.
  • Mesh-aware. A vertex mesh cannot show a wave shorter than about three of its cells. Instead of aliasing into blocky patterns, such waves are faded out (between 2.5 and 4 cells) and the tab says how many. Fine detail needs a higher Mesh resolution (up to 256), a smaller body, or longer waves.

3. Presets#

Group Presets
Still Calm Lake, Pond, Swimming Pool
Coast Tropical Lagoon
Inland River, Swamp
Sea Open Sea, Storm

Each is a graph you can open and edit. Tested properties: every preset builds valid water, the storm is taller than the sea which is taller than the lake, a stormier sea has a lower foam threshold, seeds change the waves, and no preset contains a wave its mesh cannot show.

4. Engine side (C ABI v7)#

  • NaturalFluidComponent gained customWaveCount and customWaves[16][6], appended at the end: older scenes load unchanged (the serialiser copies the common prefix) and tests cover it. With custom waves the component uses them instead of the generated wind spectrum (WaveSettings::explicitWaves; the dispersion relation fills in the missing angular frequency).
  • CaffeineWater (POD, up to 16 CaffeineWaterWave) with caffeine_session_set_water, caffeine_session_water and caffeine_session_water_height. The Rust doppio-engine crate wraps them as Water, WaterWave, Engine::set_water/water/water_height.
  • caffeine_session_tick now steps natural fluids, and the editor ticks the engine while a water surface is in the scene, so the surface animates in the viewport (the runtime app already did this).
  • Waves run on the GPU. The surface used to be rebuilt on the CPU every frame (a 256 x 256 grid sampled against 16 waves, normals included, then re-uploaded: about 28 ms per frame at 256 x 256). Now an analytic sea is a flat grid uploaded once; water.vert evaluates the Gerstner sum (the same maths as WaveField::sample, so water_height agrees with what you see) and the CPU cost per frame is about zero. The culling box is padded by the wave amplitude and choppiness (MeshGeometryComponent::boundsPadding). Surfaces with shallow-water physics or more than 16 waves keep the CPU mesh, as before.
  • Water look in the shader (scene_lit.frag, enabled for water surfaces): two layers of procedural ripple normals that fade out with distance (the fine, chaotic detail a displaced mesh cannot show), depth colour (turquoise shallows when looking down, deep blue at grazing angles), whitecaps from the wave Jacobian (crests that compress), broken up by noise, and sun glints from the ripples on the glossy surface. The body is still the PBR transparent path with the retuned low F0 and thin clearcoat.

Artefacts that were fixed (and why they cannot come back)#

What you sawCauseFix and guard
Thin straight bright lines forming a grid across the water The ripple normals came from value noise with a smooth blend. Its slope is exactly zero along every lattice line, so each line is a flat, mirror-bright stripe in a field of tilted ripples. Ripples are now gradient (Perlin) noise with an integer hash, every octave rotated so no two lattices line up. There is no slope-free line left.
Large smooth black patches with hard, scalloped edges (very visible in the Storm) The screen-space reflection trace of the water read last frame's depth and colour. Water writes no depth, so the trace hit stale or black pixels, and the patch edge followed the screen border. Water takes no screen-space reflection: it reflects the sky/probe only. The mirror direction is also kept above the horizon (R.y = abs(R.y)) so a tilted ripple never samples the dark ground half of the environment. Guard: storm_water_has_no_dark_reflection_patches renders the sea then the storm and checks that the darkest 5 % of the frame stays within 72 % of the median (it was 64 % before the fix, 81 % after).
Crests that fold over themselves Scale (choppiness above 1) and Merge can push sum(Q k A) past 1. The final wave list is scaled so sum(Q k A) ≤ 0.95, both in the editor (limit_total_steepness) and in the engine for authored waves (WaveField::configure). Guard: a C++ test with eight over-steep waves checks the Jacobian and the normal stay positive on a grid of points.

The trade-off: because water takes no screen-space reflection, objects standing in the water are not mirrored in it yet. A planar reflection pass for water is the way to get them (listed below).

5. Agents and scripting#

The tab is a pane like the others (editor.pane.water_generator, watergen.* ids). Headless: fixture water (reset takes a preset, e.g. Storm); no engine is needed for the graph and preview. Placement and animation are covered by engine-backed tests.

6. Limits and roadmap#

Reference targets and what they say about the gap#

Four references frame where water has to get to. They are context, not assets: the images are not stored here.

  1. A sculpted block of stylised sea (layered, folding, glossy turquoise-to-blue crests). Real water is not uniform: waves overtake, steepen, fold and break against each other, and the colour moves with depth and angle. Our graphs are a sum of 16 regular Gerstner waves, which is smooth and periodic; at a distance it reads as a repeating pattern. It needs irregular, non-repeating energy: a real spectrum with many more components (FFT), noise-driven amplitude and direction that vary over space, wave groups, and breaking/foam where crests fold.
  2. A pool cut-away with caustics (bright net-like light patterns on the floor and walls, a sphere floating in the surface). Water is a volume: the interesting light happens under the surface, so it needs depth-based absorption, refraction and caustics, plus walls and a floor to receive them.
  3. A rubber duck on a simulated surface, annotated: water simulation, object interaction, reflection, god rays, shadow, caustic. These are the layers a complete system has, and the objects both float and disturb the water. That is two-way coupling (displacement and impulses from bodies into the height field), which the engine's shallow-water solver can provide.
  4. A top-down ripple from an impact (concentric rings that interfere, caustic filaments, a brighter rim). Ripples are a simulation, not a sum of fixed waves: they spread from a point, reflect from edges, interfere and fade. Gerstner waves cannot make them; a height-field solver (shallow water or a wave equation on a grid) driven by drops and moving objects can.

What this changes in the roadmap, in order:

  • Chaos before polish. Add spatially varying and non-repeating waves: an FFT/spectrum ocean node with many hundreds of components, noise-modulated amplitude and direction (so no two patches look alike), wave groups and breaking foam. A hand-built Wind Sea of 8-12 waves will always look tidy.
  • Water as a volume. Depth-based absorption and colour, refraction of what is under the surface, caustics projected on floors and walls, and god rays. A water body then needs a container shape (pool, basin, shoreline), not only a flat rectangle.
  • A simulation layer next to the waves. A height-field solver node (drops, impacts, rain, boundary reflection) added on top of the analytic waves; objects add buoyancy and push the surface back (two-way interaction), with water_height already available for the first half.
  • Detail without vertices. Normal-map layers and a dedicated water shader for the fine, chaotic ripples that a displaced mesh cannot show (see the mesh limit below).
  • Reflection and shadow. Planar/screen-space reflection tuned for water, and the shadow of floating objects on the water and the floor under it.

Limits of the current implementation#

This is the foundation of the rework, not all of it. Honest status:

  • The water shading is a mode of the lit shader, not a full water shader. Done: ripple detail, depth-ish colour from the view angle, whitecaps, GPU waves. Still missing: true depth-based absorption (it needs the floor depth), refraction with a floor, shoreline foam, caustics, god rays, and the Look node's colour does not yet vary over depth, and no reflection of objects (see the table above: the screen-space trace is off for water, a planar reflection pass is the fix). The editor grid shows through clear water (it is part of the refracted scene).
  • Vertex-displaced grid, up to 256 x 256 cells (a few thousand quads cost nothing now; the grid is no longer rebuilt). A clipmap/LOD mesh around the camera is what lets an ocean reach the horizon with the detail near you; waves are already plain data for it.
  • Orbit-free preview: the tab previews the surface top-down; the 3D look is in the viewport after Place.
  • No FFT ocean node, no flow maps (rivers are stretched waves, not advected), no interactive ripples from objects yet (the shallow-water solver exists in the engine and is the way to get them), no buoyancy component, and water bodies are flat rectangles (no shorelines or islands).
  • One water colour per body; a Look cannot vary over depth until the shader lands.
  • The Nature Generator can scatter plants and rocks at the edges once bodies have shorelines.

7. Regenerating the images#

bash
./scripts/capture-water-docs.sh                                   # the tab (headless, no engine)
DOPPIO_WATER_DUMP=/tmp/water cargo test -p doppio-ui --lib water_presets_render   # engine renders of every preset

The material is an asset from the start#

The Water Material node is a mould. Applying a preset (or placing) writes Water/<name>.mat into the project and turns the node into Your Water Material (.mat) pointing at it. An existing file is never overwritten, so repainting it in the Material tab, or pointing the node at your own .mat, sticks. The terrain's splat layers are still shaded by the engine; making them project materials needs an engine change and is on the list.

Opening old .water files#

A graph saved before the material was required has no Water Material node. It gets the default one wired into the Output when it loads, so it builds again; apply or place to turn it into the project's .mat. Graphs saved with Your Water Material keep their .mat path (stored with the graph, spaces escaped).

Using it in a world#

In the World Composer a water line names a *.generator.water recipe and says where the water is: follow flow min 0.8 for a river along the terrain's flow mask (with carve <metres> to dig its bed) or fill basins level 0.18 for a lake in the basins under a normalised level. The composer then writes the water_distance mask, so classes can grow reeds only at the bank.
